title: Normalized Rewards for Preference Optimization
claim: Standard preference optimization lowers total likelihood and spuriously inflates unseen outputs; conserving likelihood mass keeps unseen outputs unaffected.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right, central preference data branching to top/bottom outcomes
description: A left-to-right toy example with three columns. On the left, a rounded box titled "Prior to DPO" shows a reference model feeding three colored response tiles A (red), B (yellow) and C (purple) with likelihoods 0.4, 0.3, 0.3, plus a blue bar chart of probabilities. A central box shows the preference data A < B, with C not present. Two gray arrows branch from it to the top and bottom. The top path, "After DPO Step", has bullets saying both likelihoods decrease and C's probability rises spuriously. It leads to an optimized-model box with A and B at 0.1 and 0.2, a red bar for C, and a sad emoji. The bottom path, "After N-DPO Step", says likelihood transfers from A to B and C is unaffected. It leads to likelihoods 0.2 and 0.5, a green bar for C, and a party emoji.
caption: Illustrative example of likelihood displacement and how our regularization mitigates it. The reference model assigns likelihoods 0.4, 0.3, 0.3 to responses $A$, $B$, $C$, with matching probabilities since the partition function equals 1. We then train on the single preference $A<B$; the response $C$ is never observed. The example highlights the distinction between unnormalized likelihoods and normalized probabilities: under DPO, the likelihoods of both $A$ and $B$ decrease while $C$'s likelihood is unchanged, yet the resulting drop in the partition function spuriously inflates $C$'s probability. To counteract this, we introduce a regularization term that conserves the total likelihood over the seen pair $(A, B)$. The preference is still learned ($A$'s likelihood falls, $B$'s rises), but the partition function (and with it the probability of the unseen response $C$) is preserved.
abstract: Direct Alignment Algorithms (DAAs) such as DPO have become a common way to post-train and align LLMs with human preferences. However, DAAs have been observed to over-optimize their implicit reward model and decrease the likelihood of preferred responses. This results in a decrease in the total likelihood assigned to responses seen in the preference dataset, potentially resulting in undesirable behavior. To counteract this undesired side-effect of DAAs, we examine the effect of using objectives that add a regularization term to maintain the total length-normalized probabilities of the chosen and rejected responses. To better understand over-optimization, we investigate how response likelihood changes are distributed over the tokens with and without regularization. We find that a significant portion of the likelihood changes are due to a small set of outlier tokens, which explains how DAAs improve generation quality despite decreasing the likelihoods of chosen responses. We apply the proposed regularization to reference-based (DPO) and reference-free (SimPO) methods and find (1) improved trade-offs between generation quality and general benchmark capability and (2) improvements in reward modeling across datasets. For example, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we see both a >20% relative increase in AlpacaEval2 scores and >9% relative performance gains on general benchmarks. Additionally, we find that the added regularization term effectively mitigates the amount of displacement within preferred responses overall, and for the outlier tokens specifically, by utilizing low-likelihood tokens.
